questions.stem: You are examining Sam, 72, in the ED. His right mid and lower zones are stony dull to percussion and breath sounds there are absent. You tell the examiner which further test you will do over the dull area. Which finding would best support a pleural effusion rather than consolidation?
options: Bronchial breath sounds with whispering pectoriloquy over the dull area
Increased tactile vocal fremitus over the dull area
Reduced vocal resonance over the dull area
Trachea deviated towards the side of the dullness
questions.why: Fluid between the pleural layers dampens transmitted sound, so vocal resonance and fremitus are reduced over an effusion. Consolidated lung conducts sound better, so they are increased. A large effusion pushes the trachea away from its side.
notes: Bronchial breathing and whispering pectoriloquy point to consolidation. Over an effusion you may hear bronchial breathing only in a thin band just above the fluid level.
Tactile fremitus is increased over consolidation but reduced over fluid, which blocks the vibration reaching the chest wall.
A trachea pulled towards the dull side suggests lobar collapse or pneumonectomy. A large effusion like Sam's pushes the trachea away.

questions.stem: Sam, 72, has a large right pleural effusion up to the 2nd anterior rib, normal clotting and no anticoagulants. The registrar does an ultrasound-guided diagnostic and therapeutic pleural aspiration after consent. How much fluid should be removed at this first aspiration?
options: No more than 500 mL, to limit the risk of pneumothorax
No more than about 1.5 L, stopping earlier if he gets cough or chest tightness
About 3 L, because the effusion reaches the 2nd anterior rib
Drain to dryness, so the CT can show the underlying lung clearly
questions.why: Remove no more than about 1.5 L at one time, and stop sooner if cough, chest tightness or pain develops. Draining more quickly risks re-expansion pulmonary oedema. Contrast CT is ideally done before full drainage.
notes: 500 mL is too cautious for a large symptomatic effusion and gives less relief than needed. Pneumothorax risk depends on technique and ultrasound guidance, not this volume limit.
Removing 3 L at once greatly raises the risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema, however big the effusion.
Draining to dryness risks re-expansion oedema, and CT is better done with some fluid in place so the pleura can be assessed.

questions.stem: Sam, 72, has COPD and SpO2 92% on room air. The nurse asks why you won't just put him on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. In a patient with COPD, what is the main mechanism by which high-concentration oxygen raises the PaCO2?
options: Suppression of hypoxic ventilatory drive from the peripheral chemoreceptors
Oxygen toxicity damaging the alveoli and reducing CO2 diffusion
Greater haemoglobin affinity for CO2 as haemoglobin becomes fully saturated
Release of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening V/Q mismatch
questions.why: High FiO2 removes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, so blood flows to poorly ventilated alveoli. This increases physiological dead space and V/Q mismatch. The Haldane effect adds to it, and loss of hypoxic drive matters much less. This is why the TSANZ target is 88 to 92%.
notes: Loss of hypoxic drive is the classic explanation, but minute ventilation barely falls. It is a minor contributor, not the main mechanism.
Oxygen toxicity needs prolonged exposure to a very high FiO2 and does not cause the rapid rise in CO2 seen in COPD.
This reverses the Haldane effect: oxygenated haemoglobin binds less CO2, so more CO2 is released into the plasma and PaCO2 rises.

questions.stem: The registrar is preparing an ultrasound-guided aspiration of Sam's large right pleural effusion through a lateral intercostal space. You are asked where the needle should pass in relation to the ribs to avoid the intercostal neurovascular bundle. Where should it go?
options: Just above the upper border of the rib below the chosen space
Just below the lower border of the rib above the chosen space
Midway between the two ribs, whatever the site of entry
Onto the rib first, then walked off its lower edge
questions.why: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, top to bottom) run in the costal groove on the inferior border of each rib. Inserting the needle just over the superior border of the rib below avoids them. Posteriorly, near the spine, the vessels are tortuous and less protected.
notes: This is where the bundle runs, in the costal groove under the rib above, so it risks bleeding from the intercostal artery and nerve injury.
Collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below, and near the spine the main vessels may cross mid-space. The safe line is just above the lower rib.
Walking off the lower edge of a rib puts the needle straight into the costal groove and the neurovascular bundle.
